assertions.text: Trigger detection, shipment optimisation, and companion constraint are in separate tables. Not one monolithic table.
assertions.evidence: "Looking at the domain you've described, I see three distinct concerns that each deserve their own table: 1. **Shipment grouping** — what triggers a split 2. **Warehouse allocation** — which warehouses to pick 3. **Companion product constraint** — keeping paired items together"

assertions.text: At least one row where multiple triggers fire simultaneously (e.g. mixed fulfilment AND mixed stock status).
assertions.evidence: Table 1, Row 8: "Different address and different fulfillment type" shows items with "Home delivery, Store pickup, Home delivery" fulfillment types across different addresses ("123 Main St, Store A, 456 Oak Ave") with split reason listed as "Fulfillment + address"

assertions.text: All four split triggers are covered: mixed fulfilment, mixed stock status, no single warehouse has all items, different addresses.
assertions.evidence: Table 1 explicitly covers: mixed fulfillment (Row 3), mixed stock status (Row 4, Row 6), and different addresses (Row 7). However, the response states its triggers as "what triggers a split (fulfillment type, availability, address)" — only three triggers — and does not include a row where the sole reason for splitting is that 'no single warehouse has all items'. This concept appears in Table 2 (warehouse allocation) but not in Table 1 (trigger detection)

assertions.text: The 'no warehouse has both companions' case is included and recognised as a product decision — e.g. flagged as an open question, or the chosen resolution is explained. Not silently omitted.
assertions.evidence: Table 3, Row 2: "Companions only available at separate warehouses" with result "no — unavoidable". This case is further addressed in the open question below the table: "When a companion pair cannot ship together (unavoidable split), do both items still ship, or is the whole companion pair held until they can go together?"

assertions.text: Companion constraint covers at least: companions at same location, companions split from non-companion items, and the ambiguous case (no location has both).
assertions.evidence: Table 3 includes all three cases: Row 1 ("Companions available at same warehouse" — companions at same location), Row 4 ("Non-companion item forces companion to split warehouse" — companions split from non-companion items), and Row 2 ("Companions only available at separate warehouses" — ambiguous case where no location has both)

assertions.text: Optimisation scenarios describe the business situation (e.g. 'Consolidate: two beats three', 'Everything at one warehouse') — not 'Test case 2'.
assertions.evidence: Table 2 scenario names are: "Single warehouse covers full order", "Exact match at one warehouse", "Two warehouses needed, optimal pair exists", "Three warehouses needed, no better combination", "Suboptimal allocation avoided", "One warehouse has surplus — no split needed", "Total stock across all warehouses insufficient", "Exact stock spread across many warehouses" — all descriptive business situations

assertions.text: The trigger table represents multi-item orders where each item has its own fulfillment type, address, and availability. The notation used makes the item-to-property mapping unambiguous — not value sets like {delivery, pickup} which lose which item has which property.
assertions.evidence: Table 1, Row 3: "Shirt, Book" with fulfillment types "Home delivery, Store pickup" clearly maps the first item (Shirt) to the first property (Home delivery) and the second item (Book) to the second property (Store pickup). Similarly, Row 7 shows "Shirt, Book" with addresses "123 Main St, 456 Oak Ave" preserving the per-item mapping by position

assertions.text: Optimisation table uses a scalar count column (e.g. 'Shirts ordered') not item lists, when product identity doesn't matter for the logic.
assertions.evidence: Table 2 uses scalar columns: the "Item" column contains the scalar value "Shirt" (repeated across all rows) and the "Qty ordered" column contains scalar values "4", "3", "6", "6", "6", "4", "10", "4" — not item lists or property sets

assertions.text: Inventory assignments are physically valid: items are only assigned to locations that have them. Shipment counts match the assignments shown.
assertions.evidence: Table 2, Row 3: "Shirt × 6 needed" with "Philadelphia: 3, Washington: 3" selected warehouses = 3 + 3 = 6 units, producing "2 shipments". Row 5 shows "Shirt × 6" with Philadelphia: 3, Washington: 3 selected = 6 units, 2 shipments. All rows show valid assignments matching inventory availability and shipment counts

assertions.text: @DisplayName is present on test methods, OR method names read as clear descriptive titles when converted from camelCase/snake_case.
assertions.evidence: The response is a design document providing tables and scenario descriptions but does not include @DisplayName annotations or method name definitions. Scenario names like "Single in-stock home delivery" appear only within table rows, not as method-level declarations

assertions.text: @Description is present on at least the class and provides context beyond what the table rows already express — such as the splitting rules, constraints, or application context. Does NOT merely restate the column names or summarise what the rows show.
assertions.evidence: The response does not include @Description annotations on any class or methods. While it provides narrative context (opening explanation of three concerns, 'Open questions' sections, final paragraph on companion/minimisation priority), these are not formatted as @Description annotations as the assertion requires

assertions.text: Annotations appear in order: @DisplayName (if present), @Description (if present), @TableTest — not any other order.
assertions.evidence: The response is a design document without any Java annotations. No @DisplayName, @Description, @TableTest, or other annotations are present; therefore the order cannot be verified and the assertion cannot be satisfied

assertions.text: If @Description is present and the text is longer than a single short line, it uses a text block (triple-quoted string """), not string concatenation with +. Passes if @Description is absent.
assertions.evidence: @Description is not present in the response, and the assertion explicitly states "Passes if @Description is absent"
